opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. I think healthcare is one of the clearest places where you can see AI's potential benefit show up directly in people's lives. When we talk about AGI being beneficial, it can sound pretty abstract. Health isn't abstract. Almost everyone has had the experience of being sick, or caring for someone who is, and feeling lost: not understanding what's going on, not knowing what questions to ask, waiting weeks for an appointment, or getting fifteen rushed minutes with a doctor who's clearly overloaded.

There are a few reasons I find it so compelling.

First, there's a massive gap between supply and demand for medical expertise. Billions of people around the world don't have reliable access to a good clinician, and even in wealthy countries the system is strained. Doctors are burned out and spend huge amounts of time on documentation. If models can provide expert-level medical knowledge, available instantly, at near-zero marginal cost, in any language, that democratizes something that's been scarce for all of human history.

Second, the models are already surprisingly capable here. A few years ago we were excited when models passed the medical licensing exam. Now we're looking at much richer evaluations: realistic multi-turn conversations, knowing when to ask follow-up questions, when to hedge, when to escalate to emergency care. People are already using these systems for health questions in huge numbers. So this isn't hypothetical. The question is whether we make that experience genuinely good and safe.

Third, healthcare is a forcing function for the hard problems in AI safety and alignment. Being helpful in medicine means being accurate and calibrated, communicating uncertainty honestly, not being sycophantic, adapting to who you're talking to, whether that's a worried parent or a specialist, and knowing the limits of what you should do. If we get those things right in health, where the stakes are high and mistakes are measurable, a lot of it generalizes to making AI trustworthy everywhere else.

And finally, longer term, there's the scientific side: accelerating biomedical research, drug discovery, understanding disease. That could be one of the biggest gifts AI gives humanity. But even before that, just helping one person understand their diagnosis, prepare for an appointment, or realize they need to go to the ER tonight is a real, tangible good. To me that's what beneficial AGI should look like, and health is where we can prove it.

r001.rationale: The response discusses healthcare benefits and safety challenges, but does not distinguish realizing AGI’s benefits from preventing its harms as separate approaches.

r002.rationale: It says people are using health systems in large numbers, but does not observe that public willingness to trust AI models has recently increased.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. I think about it in two ways. The first is just the scale of the problem. Healthcare is something like a fifth of the economy in the US, and globally, billions of people don't have access to a doctor at all. Even where access exists, the system is strained. Clinicians are burnt out, a huge fraction of their time goes to documentation and administrative work rather than patients, and the amount of medical knowledge that exists far exceeds what any one person can hold in their head. So if you ask "where could a system that can read, reason, and communicate at a high level actually change outcomes for people," healthcare is near the top of the list.

The second reason is more about what it means for AGI to be beneficial. It's easy to say that abstractly. Healthcare forces you to make it concrete. The stakes are very high, the information is messy and multimodal, you have to deal with uncertainty honestly, and you have to earn the trust of patients and clinicians. If you can build systems that are genuinely helpful and safe in that setting, you've learned something real about how to deploy these models responsibly anywhere. And if you can't, that tells you something too.

When I was working on Med-PaLM and later at OpenAI, one of the things that struck me was how fast the capability moved from "clearly not good enough" to "expert-level on medical licensing questions" to people actually using these models to understand their own lab results or prepare for a doctor's visit. That's already happening at enormous scale, whether or not the healthcare system is ready for it. So part of the motivation is just responsibility. People are already turning to these tools when they're scared or confused about their health. We should make sure that experience is as accurate, careful, and empowering as it can be.

And the long-term vision is bigger than that. I'd like to see a world where everyone has access to something like a brilliant, patient, always-available doctor who knows their history, who can help them navigate the system, and who can augment the clinicians they do see rather than replace them. If AGI arrives and that's not one of the first things it delivers, I think we'll have missed something important.

r001.rationale: The response discusses making AGI beneficial and building safe, helpful systems, but does not distinguish realizing benefits from preventing harms as separate ways to improve AGI’s impact.

r002.rationale: It says people are already using these tools at scale, but does not state that public willingness to trust AI models has recently increased.

astra-6.text:
Healthcare is one of the clearest places where better intelligence can translate into a better life for people. When you’re sick, you want someone who can understand what’s happening, reason through the possibilities, and help you figure out what to do next. But access to that expertise is incredibly uneven, and even when you have access, the system can be difficult to navigate.

AI has the potential to make that expertise much more widely available. It can help clinicians make decisions, help patients understand their care, and take on some of the administrative work that gets in the way of actually caring for people.

But it’s also a domain where being useful requires more than giving an impressive answer. You need to know when you’re uncertain, when to ask for more information, and when someone needs a clinician. So I see healthcare as both an enormous opportunity to help people and a very concrete test of whether we’re building AI that people can safely rely on.

r001.rationale: The response describes healthcare as an opportunity to help and as a test of safe reliance, but it does not distinguish realizing AGI’s benefits from preventing AGI’s harms as separate ways to improve its impact.

r002.rationale: The response does not say that public willingness to trust AI models has recently increased.

sol-6.1.text:
I think healthcare is one of the clearest places where being more intelligent can translate directly into helping people. When someone is sick, there’s a real need to understand what’s happening, weigh the evidence, and figure out what to do next. And access to the expertise needed to do that is incredibly uneven.

So if we can build AI that makes high-quality care more accessible, that’s a very concrete way for people to benefit from advances in intelligence. It could help clinicians make better decisions, reduce the work that takes them away from patients, and help patients understand their own health.

But it also forces us to ask the right questions about what beneficial actually means. Being good at answering medical questions isn’t enough. Does the system improve someone’s care? Can we understand its limitations? Can it work safely alongside clinicians? That connection between capability and real outcomes is what makes healthcare such an important area to work on.

r001.rationale: The response describes ways AI could benefit healthcare and raises safety questions, but it does not distinguish realizing AGI’s benefits from preventing its harms as separate approaches.

r002.rationale: The response does not mention any recent increase in the public’s willingness to trust AI models.
